title: SDK call tracing and root-cause playbook
author: Sofia Lin
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook describes a standardized approach for instrumenting Redwood SDKs, propagating trace/correlation identifiers, and performing fast root-cause analysis when customer requests fail or show degraded latency. It consolidates client-side examples, server-side expectations, console lookup patterns, and a prioritized troubleshooting checklist.

Audience:
- SDK engineers (Python, TypeScript/Node, Java)
- Backend engineers integrating Redwood APIs
- SREs and support engineers performing customer triage

Scope and goals:
- Ensure every SDK call can be correlated to a single trace or a small set of related traces in Redwood Console.
- Define minimal headers and span attributes to set in SDKs so SREs can diagnose errors without asking customers for payloads.
- Provide a compact runbook for reproducing, isolating, and escalating issues within 30 minutes.

Quick summary (one-line): Include an idempotent correlation_id on every user request, propagate trace/span headers, sample 1% of requests with full debug traces, and attach trace IDs to errors and telemetry emitted by the SDK.

Minimum tracing contract (what SDKs must implement)
1) Correlation headers: every outgoing HTTP request from SDK must set:
   - X-Request-Id: a UUID v4 (string) representing the client request lifecycle.
   - X-Traceparent: W3C Trace Context header (if available) for interoperability.
   - X-Sdk-Client: <sdk-name>/<version> (e.g. redwood-js/1.3.0)

2) Error enrichment: when an error is raised from the SDK to the customer app, the SDK should include the X-Request-Id value and the Redwood-side trace id (if received) in the error metadata.

3) Sampling and debug payloads:
   - Default sampling: 0.01 (1% full traces) for hosted customers to control cost.
   - Force-sampled flag: SDKs expose a debug override (environment variable REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true) that forces full capture and returns a debug_trace_id in responses for triage.

Header example (HTTP):
X-Request-Id: 8a7dd3e2-6f8b-4ea9-9f0b-2a9c3e5b9f0d
X-Traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
X-Sdk-Client: redwood-py/2.0.0

Recommended SDK implementation patterns
- Generate X-Request-Id at the top-level SDK API entry (e.g., client.generate_request_id()). Reuse it across retries and sub-requests spawned by the same logical call.
- If the host application provides a trace context (OpenTelemetry or W3C), prefer propagating that traceparent header instead of generating a new trace. Always attach X-Request-Id regardless.
- Avoid including user PII in correlation IDs or trace attributes. Use non-sensitive labels (e.g., user_hash, project_id).

Client examples
Python (requests):
```python
import uuid
import requests

def call_redwood(payload, api_key, force_debug=False):
    rid = str(uuid.uuid4())
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "X-Request-Id": rid,
        "X-Sdk-Client": "redwood-py/2.0.0"
    }
    if force_debug:
        headers["X-Redwood-Trace-Debug"] = "1"
    r = requests.post("https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate", json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=30)
    # Attach request id to exceptions for faster triage
    if r.status_code >= 500:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Redwood server error ({r.status_code}), request_id={rid}")
    return r.json(), rid
```

Node/TypeScript (fetch):
```ts
import {v4 as uuidv4} from 'uuid';

async function callRedwood(payload: object, apiKey: string, forceDebug = false) {
  const rid = uuidv4();
  const headers: Record<string, string> = {
    'Authorization': `Bearer ${apiKey}` ,
    'X-Request-Id': rid,
    'X-Sdk-Client': 'redwood-js/1.4.1'
  }
  if (forceDebug) headers['X-Redwood-Trace-Debug'] = '1'
  const resp = await fetch('https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    headers,
    // keep a short timeout at the application layer to avoid stuck clients
  })
  if (!resp.ok && resp.status >= 500) {
    throw new Error(`Redwood server error (${resp.status}), request_id=${rid}`)
  }
  const body = await resp.json();
  return {body, request_id: rid};
}
```

Server-side expectations (Redwood runtime)
- If incoming request includes X-Request-Id, the runtime must use it as the root-correlation-id for logs, traces, and KV-caches for that request.
- The runtime will return the header X-Redwood-Trace-Id when a full trace was captured for the request. SDKs should surface that id in error payloads.
- Runtime will also echo back X-Request-Id when present to verify propagation.

Common triage flow (30-minute runbook)
1) Gather artifacts: customer request time, X-Request-Id (or approximate timestamp), sample customer payload (if allowed), SDK name/version, region.
2) Search Console: filter by X-Request-Id or time window (+/- 2 minutes). If present, open the trace. Check service span latencies, kernel queue time, and tail token generation time.
3) If no trace found: verify if customer had client-side sampling or wrong header (common root cause). Ask customer to resend with REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true to force a debug trace.
4) If trace found and error is 5xx: inspect backend service spans in trace for exceptions and logs. Correlate with runtime logs (owner: serving-runtime team).
5) If high latency but no 5xx: check batching layer span and KV cache hit rate; correlate with GPU utilization from gpu-fleet-and-capacity dashboard.
6) Escalate: if issue is reproducible and affects Dedicated/Private customers or violates SLOs, open an Incident and notify eng-sre and serving-runtime on-call. Attach trace ids and representative payload.

Priority lookup table
| Artifact | Where to look | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| X-Request-Id | Redwood Console / request traces | SRE / support | Best single key for cross-system lookup |
| X-Redwood-Trace-Id | Trace view | Serving runtime | Indicates full capture; include in bug reports |
| SDK logs | Customer app logs | Customer / SDK-team | Ask for SDK debug logs with correlation id |
| GPU metrics | Grafana (gpu-fleet) | Infra / capacity | Helps diagnose batching/backpressure |

Canonical fixes and known patterns
- Symptom: No trace in Console but customer reports error. Cause: client stripped headers (proxies or CORS) or client used custom HTTP client without propagation. Fix: document header requirements in integration guide and add SDK instrumentation tests that assert header presence.
- Symptom: High 95th token latency. Cause: large request sequences hitting longer attention kernels or cache misses. Fix: include request size metrics and advise quantized model variants or lower max_tokens.
- Symptom: Intermittent 502/503. Cause: transient scaling/queue drains. Fix: implement exponential backoff with full jitter in SDKs (recommended default: initial=50ms, max=2s, max_retries=5).

Telemetry and logs to collect when filing a support ticket
- Timestamp (UTC), X-Request-Id, SDK name/version, region, sample payload (if customer consents), client-side logs (including stack traces), any returned X-Redwood-Trace-Id.

Debugging checklist for SDK authors (pre-release)
1) Unit tests assert X-Request-Id exists and is stable across retries.
2) Integration tests using a local proxy record all outgoing headers.
3) Optional e2e test that flips REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true and asserts the runtime returns X-Redwood-Trace-Id.
4) Add metrics emitted by the SDK for: requests_total, requests_errors_total (label: status_code), request_latency_seconds (histogram).

Escalation and ownership
- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (SDK telemetry workstream)
- On-call for runtime tracing: eng-serving-runtime on-call (see runbooks/trace-oncall).
- Severity mapping:
  - Sev-1: Reproducible data-loss or SLO breach for Dedicated customer — immediate incident.
  - Sev-2: Widespread >=10% error rate increase for hosted customers — paged to eng-sre.
  - Sev-3: Single-customer sporadic errors — support ticket and scheduled follow-up.

Appendix A: Example support ticket template (copy/paste)
Subject: [Support] Request tracing artifacts for customer <customer-name> – request_id=<X-Request-Id>
Body:
- Time (UTC):
- Region:
- SDK: (name/version)
- X-Request-Id:
- X-Redwood-Trace-Id (if present):
- Sample payload (redacted if necessary):
- Customer logs attached: yes/no
- Screenshots of Console trace: yes/no

Appendix B: Reference commands
- curl example to include headers:
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "X-Request-Id: $(uuidgen)" -H "X-Redwood-Trace-Debug: 1" -d '{"prompt":"hi"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate

- Small grep to find request_id in logs (SRE):
  rg "8a7dd3e2-6f8b" /var/log/redwood/ -n || true

Appendix C: FAQ
Q: What if a customer cannot share payloads?
A: Request only the minimal redacted payload necessary to reproduce (e.g., token counts, sequence length, prompt shape). Ask them to enable REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG for a time window; debug traces are sampled and limited to triage windows.

Q: Is X-Request-Id globally unique across retries?
A: Yes — keep the same id for retries of the same logical call to simplify dedup and tracing.
